name: The Bunya-Bunya of Jardim da Cordoaria

location.address: Jardim da Cordoaria (Jardim de João Chagas), Porto

story:
The tallest thing in the Jardim da Cordoaria is Australian. The bunya pine here runs to roughly 40 metres, a dark dome standing clear above the plane trees, on a straight trunk 3.6 metres round.

Araucaria bidwillii grows naturally in a few pockets of southeast Queensland and nowhere else. The leaves are stiff, glossy and sharp enough to draw blood, arranged in spirals along the branch, and the tree has a habit that made it famous at home. It drops cones the size of a football weighing several kilograms, which is why bunya groves were gathering places and why nobody sensible parks under one in season.

Local tree histories put this one in the ground between 1867 and 1869, when the garden was laid out. The register, measuring in 2004, recorded 130 years, which works out at roughly 150 today. The planting dates would make it a few years older still. Two independent routes to the same decade is about as good as tree dating gets.

It was classified in 2005, in the same decree as the avenue of plane trees a few steps away, so this small garden gives you two protected entries in one stop. Stand in the plane tunnel and look up at the far end: the araucaria is the thing breaking the roofline.

name: The Tulip Tree of Casa Allen

location.address: Jardins da Casa Allen (Casa das Artes), Rua Rúben A, 210, Porto

story:
Two official documents give this tree's waist as 5.24 metres and 7.75 metres. The register measured 5.24 at chest height in 2015. The 2021 news coverage of its classification gives 7.75 as the perimeter at the base. Both agree exactly on everything else, 31 metres tall with a 29 metre crown, so the gap is almost certainly about where the tape went rather than a disagreement about the tree.

Either way it is a big tulip tree. Liriodendron tulipifera comes from the eastern United States, where it is the tallest hardwood of the Appalachian forest, and 31 metres is a serious height for one in Europe. The leaf is the giveaway from below: four lobes with the tip cut off square, as though someone had gone at it with scissors.

No age has ever been recorded for it, by the register or by anyone else.

It grows in the garden of Casa Allen, a 1920s house by the architect José Marques da Silva, now Casa das Artes and run by the Direção Regional de Cultura do Norte. The garden is genuinely open, with guided visits alongside the exhibition rooms, but it keeps the building's hours, which on most days do not begin until half past two in the afternoon. Turning up at eleven gets you a locked gate.
access: Free, public building and gardens run by the Direção Regional de Cultura do Norte; guided garden visits offered alongside the exhibition spaces
transport: In the Massarelos district, walking distance from Palácio de Cristal and the Marquês metro/tram area

name: The Magnolia Ring of Jardim de São Lázaro

location.address: Jardim de São Lázaro, around the lake, Porto
location.neighbourhood: Cedofeita, Santo Ildefonso, Sé, Miragaia, São Nicolau e Vitória

story:
Twelve southern magnolias stand in a ring around the lake in the oldest public garden in Porto. The Jardim de São Lázaro opened in 1834, the city's first, and the magnolias came later. The register recorded them at 100 years when it measured in 2004, which puts them near 120 now and means they were planted into a garden that was already the best part of a century old.

Magnolia grandiflora is from the American southeast and is built for this job. The leaves are thick, dark and permanently glossy, with a rust-coloured felt on the underside that shows when the wind lifts them. In early summer the flowers open the size of a dinner plate, cream white, and carry the length of the lake on a still evening.

Each of the twelve has a trunk about 2.6 metres round and stands close to 16 metres tall. They were classified as a single group in 2005, which is the right way to read them: one lake, one loop of path, all twelve in view as you walk it, rather than twelve separate trees to hunt down.

Porto has other notable magnolias, including one classified only recently. This is the set arranged around water, in the garden the city opened first.

best_time.label: June and July, when all twelve open lemon-scented white flowers around the lake

name: The Camellias of Largo da Igreja de Paranhos

location.address: Largo da Igreja de Paranhos, in front of the Igreja de São Veríssimo de Paranhos, Porto

story:
Most people picture a camellia as a shrub in a pot. These two are six and a half metres tall with crowns ten metres across, and the state has had them under protection since 1992.

They stand a few metres apart in the largo in front of the Igreja de São Veríssimo de Paranhos, a working parish church with an open square, so there are no gates and no hours. The trunks are modest, 1.15 and 1.25 metres round, because a camellia puts its growth into a dense mass of branches rather than one stem. From the far side of the largo the pair reads as a single green wall with a church behind it.

Porto has traded on camellias since the 19th century, when the varieties came in through the port and the city's gardens filled with them. The register recorded these two at 200 years old when it measured in 2006, which puts them near 220 now. If that holds, they were growing here before the fashion arrived.

Beyond the register itself they have gone unwritten about. No article, no local history, no photograph that names them. For a city that calls itself the city of camellias that is an odd gap, and it is worth saying plainly that the age and the species here rest on the state's record alone.

best_time.label: January and February, when both are in full flower against the church wall

name: The Metrosideros of Passeio Alegre

location.address: Jardim do Passeio Alegre, Rua do Passeio Alegre, Porto
location.neighbourhood: Aldoar, Foz do Douro e Nevogilde

story:
Two of these stand eleven metres apart on the grass at Passeio Alegre, and neither is much taller than a house. Seven metres of height, trunks 3.15 and 2.62 metres round, crowns averaging nearly 13 metres. They are wider than they are tall, and that shape is the whole point.

Metrosideros excelsa grows on sea cliffs at home in New Zealand, anchored in rock and salt wind, and the mouth of the Douro is the closest thing Porto has to that. Aerial roots hang off the older limbs. The bark is grey and fibrous. Nothing about the tree says ornamental until late spring, when the crowns go red with stamens rather than petals, thousands at once.

The two were classified together in 2005 as isolated specimens, which is exactly how they stand: out on the open lawn rather than in the promenade's tree lines. The register recorded both at 70 years when it measured in 2004, so roughly 90 now, and the city's own environment service puts them at over 80, which agrees.

Passeio Alegre is the long formal garden at the Foz end of the waterfront, laid out in the 19th century as the place Porto came to walk on a Sunday. It is still doing that job, and these two have watched every version of it.

best_time.label: late spring, when both crowns turn red with stamens above the river mouth

name: The Seven Fan Palms of Palácio de Cristal

location.address: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, Porto

story:
The building these palms were planted for was demolished in 1951. The palms are still standing.

Seven Mexican fan palms line the Avenida das Tílias in the gardens of the Palácio de Cristal, and they date to the planting that went in around the international exhibition of 1865, the event the crystal palace itself was built for. That building came down after eighty-six years and was replaced by the domed pavilion sitting there now. The palms carried on and reach almost 25 metres.

Washingtonia robusta is from northwest Mexico and puts up a slender grey trunk far faster than most palms, topped with a crown of stiff fan-shaped leaves that clatter in wind. Seven of them in a line, all the same age, is an unusual survival. Palms at that height tend to go in storms or in redevelopment, and these have sat through both.

They were classified in 2019. The register carries the classification and an age of 150 years at its 2015 measurement, roughly 160 now, which matches the exhibition-era planting. It carries no measurements at all for this entry, so the heights here come from an independent account of the gardens rather than from the state.

The gardens are free and busy, and the peacocks have the run of them.

name: The Magnolias of Jardim de Arca d'Água

location.address: Jardim de Arca d'Água, Praça de 9 de Abril, Porto

story:
This garden holds 96 plane trees, 57 camellias and 13 southern magnolias, and only the magnolias are protected. The set was classified in 2021, which means the state looked at everything growing in the Jardim de Arca d'Água and singled out the smallest group in it.

Finding them takes a minute of looking. The garden covers 22,000 square metres and the register gives one coordinate standing in for all thirteen, so the pin here points at the garden rather than at the trees. They are not hard to pick out once you are inside. Magnolia grandiflora has thick dark leaves with a rust-brown felt on the underside, quite unlike the planes and the camellias around them, and in early summer the flowers are the size of a plate.

No age is recorded for them. The register gives one representative trunk at 2.43 metres round and leaves the rest blank, so the honest answer is that nobody has dated these trees.

The garden opened in 1928 in Paranhos, on ground named for its arca de água, the stone chamber where a spring is captured and held. The springs here supplied Porto with water for centuries before anyone thought to lay a bandstand and a playground over them.
access: Free, public municipal garden with playground, lake and bandstand
transport: Paranhos, close to the Asprela / hospital and university cluster; served by Porto metro Line D and STCP buses

name: The Alameda dos Plátanos of Jardim da Cordoaria

location.address: Jardim da Cordoaria (Jardim de João Chagas), Porto

story:
The state protected this one as a tunnel rather than as thirty-seven trees. The Alameda dos Plátanos runs through the Jardim da Cordoaria in central Porto, its plane trees trained until the crowns closed overhead, and the classification of 2005 treats the whole avenue as one thing of public interest.

That is the right reading. Walked separately these are ordinary London planes, 19 metres tall, carrying the flaking camouflage bark the species is known for. Walked together they make a green corridor with the light coming through in patches, which is why the avenue turns up in photographs of Porto far more often than any single tree in the garden.

The register measured in 2004 and recorded 140 years, putting the avenue near 160 now. An independent survey of Porto's classified trees calls it more than 150 years old and gives the same 19 metre height, so the two figures agree.

The garden was a rope walk before it was a garden, a long open strip where cordage was laid out and twisted, which is where the name Cordoaria comes from and why the space still runs in long lines. Stand in the tunnel and look up at the far end. The dark dome breaking the roofline is the bunya pine, classified in the same decree on the same day.

name: The Tulip Trees of Praça Pedro Nunes

location.address: Praça Pedro Nunes, next to the former Liceu D. Manuel II, Porto
location.neighbourhood: Cedofeita, Santo Ildefonso, Sé, Miragaia, São Nicolau e Vitória

story:
Praça Pedro Nunes is small enough to cross in twenty seconds and holds four tulip trees, each about 22 metres tall. They were classified together as one group in 2005, standing beside the former Liceu D. Manuel II, and generations of pupils came out of that building into their shade.

Liriodendron tulipifera is worth identifying from the pavement. The leaf looks as though someone cut the tip off with scissors, four lobes and a flat top, unlike anything else growing on a Porto square. The flowers are genuinely tulip-shaped, greenish yellow with an orange band, and genuinely hard to see, because they open high in the crown in early summer and face upward.

The register measured in 2004: trunks 3.6 metres round, 22 metres tall, crowns 17 metres across, and an age of 80, which puts the group near 100 now.

One thing to know before going. The register and a 2005 survey of Porto's classified trees are the only records of this group, and no recent article or dated photograph confirms that all four are still there. Four large trees in a central square are unlikely to have gone quietly, but the last written confirmation is twenty years old, and anyone standing in the square can settle it faster than any archive.
